fields_add.community: The Bank's own completion report of 13 February 2018 on the grant, IDA-H6990 of XDR 32.8 million or US$52 million equivalent, records that the project's involuntary resettlement compliance rating was Satisfactory at the start, was downgraded to Highly Unsatisfactory at the mid-term review, which brought the overall project rating down with it, and stood at Moderately Unsatisfactory at closing, the report recording that by the close of the project the rating was progressively upgraded from Highly Unsatisfactory to Unsatisfactory to Moderately Unsatisfactory, largely because of improvements in carrying out the Aynak plan, with better documentation of grievance intake, discrepancies in the names of project-affected persons clarified and a stronger understanding of the use of community organisers. The downgrade was based on the Ministry of Mines and Petroleum's slow and faltering implementation of the Aynak Resettlement Action Plan, its failure to observe the policies and procedures set out in that plan and in the project's Environmental and Social Management Framework as reflected in the financing agreement, poor handling of grievance redress and of reporting and documentation, and slow re-staffing of the Ministry's Social Adviser post. The report states that the information given to the Bank on resettlement was 'sparse and confusing', with limited connection between the plan and the project-affected persons named in it. The same passage records that, on the Ministry's own report, it had gone ahead with land acquisition and compensation for an access road close to the mine site without following due process: no household survey, no identification of losses and no second resettlement plan. Two deficiencies were still open at closing: the Ministry could not procure a water pump for the new township and resettlement site, which the report calls a barrier to completing the resettlement, and there was no agreement on the final list of people entitled to the various levels of compensation. A footnote to the same section says the Bank's safeguard procedures were simply not aligned with government laws, rules and procedures on land acquisition, and that where possible the laws and regulations were circumvented through a presidential decree, which took enormous effort and time and was not always within the control of the Aynak authority. At closing the Bank team was still seeking clarification from the land authority ARAZI on how it classified the categories of people eligible for compensation at Aynak.
fields_add.outcome: A project preparation grant attached to a later Bank operation took over responsibility for carrying out the Mes Aynak resettlement plan.

rogun-stage1-resettlement.community: The resettlement plan prepared under the Bank-financed assessment identifies 289 households, a population of 2,048 making up 527 families, as project-affected people in the seven Stage 1 villages, on the basis of the 2011 census. All of them lose their house plots and their agricultural and pasture land. Among them, 38 household heads are women, three of those widows; 31 people are disabled, 22 men and 9 women; 23 household heads are disabled; and 12 households, 4.1 per cent, were found to be very poor. The plan records that resettlement at Rogun started more than 30 years ago, was interrupted by the civil war and resumed, and that it was decided not to interrupt the process for the Stage 1 villages, so moves continued while the plan was being written. A table of families already resettled as of June 2011 gives 20 at Rudaki against an intended 286, 70 at Dangara against 250, 100 at Tursunzade against 367, 35 at Darband against 15,000 and none at Chormagzak against 67; the plan notes that this table does not distinguish families from the Stage 1 and Stage 2 villages and gives no total. As of end September 2011, 24 families from Sicharog Jamoat in Rogun district had moved to the new sites. Of the Stage 1 villages, 230 graves had to be relocated. The plan's own household survey records the loss of fruit and timber trees as the main negative aspect of the move, followed by a lack of funds to build the new houses, then the loss of agricultural land, with 14 per cent of respondents reporting difficulties in moving and 10 per cent regretting leaving the place they were born; the main positive aspects given were a constant supply of electricity, the prospect of new jobs and better housing. The plan then sets out the main points of the Bureau for Human Rights report described below, beginning with the statement that in general the majority of the people are satisfied with the way resettlement is handled by the government organisations, and listing the complaints that report recorded. Valuation of most properties, mainly houses, was carried out in 2009 while compensation was paid later, when people started building at the new site, and prices for construction material and labour had risen in the meantime without the compensation amount taking that into account. Compensation was paid in stages beginning with 30 per cent when construction started, which caused problems for many households, who asked for payment in full or at least 70 per cent up front. Payment went only to the owner of the structure, as a rule the household head, although many households contained several families, so other families living with the owner had to build at their own expense. No special provisions were being made for households headed by women, for disabled or for elderly people. People living near the dam in the risk zone faced inconvenience and danger from construction. House plots of 1,000 square metres at the new sites were said to be insufficient for large households. Transport of movable assets to the new site was provided but was often not enough for all possessions, especially livestock, so many people had to sell some of their animals. Complaints were made about the information given and the chance to take part in decisions, and about water supply, road conditions and schools at the new sites. The plan adds that many of the relocated households mentioned the availability and fertility of agricultural land at the new sites at Tursunzade, Rudaki and Dangara, and that nobody complained of a lack of land or of access to it. An early resettlement audit found that compensation amounts needed updating to replacement cost and to account for inflation, that vulnerable groups needed special support with house construction, transport and livelihood restoration, that transport capacity for moving all movable assets including livestock was insufficient, and that a structure was needed on the ground to improve public participation; the plan says the Resettlement Unit had begun building those recommendations into its daily practice. The Dushanbe non-governmental organisation Bureau for Human Rights and Rule of Law, working under an EU assignment, evaluated the resettlement in parallel and its report is quoted at length in the Bank-disclosed plan: there is no independent property valuation institution in Tajikistan, most housing was assessed in 2009 and the assessed value was not enough to build decent housing by 2011, the staged 30 per cent payments left residents who had spent the first instalment unable to build and mostly unemployed, people lacked clear information on relocation and on how complaints would be handled, and some new areas still had no power lines, water supply, schools, kindergartens, medical facilities or roads despite a legal requirement to put those in before relocation; the same seven conclusions also state that in most cases people were willing to move and consented, while the oldest residents and people with disabilities wanted to stay where they were or move nearby. Human Rights Watch, reporting on 25 June 2014 from 156 interviews carried out between November 2013 and February 2014, states that the government resettled about 1,500 families from 2009 onward, that resettlement sites are often more than 100 km from the original villages and some families were moved as far as 200 km, that families said compensation was too low to replace their homes, that agricultural land was not available in all resettled communities, that families spent more on food and lost farming and livestock income, that some new communities had no school and children walked up to two hours to class, and that blasting near the site damaged homes.
rogun-stage1-resettlement.displaced_note: ICIJ gives 2,048 for this project, which is its count of project-affected people and not a count of people moved. The Stage 1 Resettlement Action Plan states that a total of 289 households, whose population is 2,048, making up 527 families, were identified as project-affected people from the 2011 census. The plan's own table of families already resettled by June 2011 gives four site figures of 20, 70, 100 and 35, with none at a fifth site, and states that the table does not separate Stage 1 from Stage 2 families; the plan gives no total of people moved. Human Rights Watch puts the number resettled from 2009 onward at about 1,500 families, which covers the dam as a whole and not only Stage 1.
rogun-stage1-resettlement.outcome: The project closed on 31 December 2014 having paid for the assessment studies and not for construction or resettlement. The Bank's completion report of 29 June 2015 rated the outcome Moderately Satisfactory, risk to development outcome Moderate, Bank performance Satisfactory and borrower performance Moderately Satisfactory. The Independent Evaluation Group's review ICRR14942, posted 9 June 2016, gave outcome Moderately Satisfactory, risk to development outcome Significant, Bank performance Moderately Satisfactory and borrower performance Moderately Satisfactory. The Project Performance Assessment Report of 27 July 2020 lowered those to outcome Moderately Unsatisfactory, risk to development outcome High, Bank performance Unsatisfactory and borrower performance Moderately Unsatisfactory. That report also records that the Bank opted not to finance Rogun, that the assessment process helped the Government make the case for raising finance through Eurobonds in 2017 to start work on the dam, and that the first two of six planned turbines were launched by the end of 2019.

rogun-stage1-resettlement.confidence_note: The Bank did not pay for the dam or for the resettlement. The credit, the additional financing grant and the Swiss grant paid for the Rogun assessment studies, and the completion report states that those three instruments 'did not fund any construction related activities under the project'; the Project Performance Assessment Report says the project 'purposefully excluded financing of construction for the Rogun HEP'. What the money did pay for includes the Environmental and Social Impact Assessment, the Stage 1 Resettlement Action Plan and the Resettlement Audit, and the completion report records that the Bank advised the Government on the resettlement instruments and monitored the resettlement, work it says continued after the project closed. The household and population counts, the figures for families already moved, the complaints and the audit findings come from the resettlement plan and policy framework the credit financed and the Bank disclosed, so on those the Bank is reporting on an instrument it paid for. The complaints about 2009 valuations, staged payments, livestock sold and services missing at the new sites are the findings of the Bureau for Human Rights and Rule of Law, a Dushanbe organisation working under an EU assignment, as the plan reproduces them, and not a second source. Human Rights Watch is independent of both: it interviewed 156 people in the resettled communities between November 2013 and February 2014 and reports compensation too low to replace homes, agricultural land missing in some communities, higher food costs and lost farming and livestock income, communities without a school, and blasting damage to homes. Its figure of about 1,500 families resettled from 2009 covers the dam as a whole, not Stage 1, and no document reconciles it with the plan's counts; the plan's own table of families already moved does not separate Stage 1 from Stage 2. The plan records that the majority of people are satisfied with how the resettlement was handled, that relocation was voluntary in most cases, and that nobody complained of a lack of agricultural land. The Inspection Panel request registered on 22 October 2010 was brought by the Ecological Movement of Uzbekistan over downstream transboundary effects of the dam, not by the resettled people, and does not bear on the resettlement.
rogun-stage1-resettlement.conditions: The Independent Evaluation Group's review sets out the sequence: the appraisal document stated that the project 'would not trigger any Safeguards policies, since it would be implemented on existing electricity and gas networks' and classified it environmental category C, a classification the additional financing project paper repeats for the original project; the completion report recognises that the original project was in fact category B, because it involved installing electricity and gas meters in existing consuming centres; and under the additional financing the category was changed to A to reflect the potential impacts of the Rogun hydroelectric project for which the assessment studies were being carried out, which is the category the completion report's data sheet records. The completion report rates safeguards Satisfactory throughout and states that the recipient and the implementing agencies were in compliance with the agreed safeguard policies under both the original grant and the additional financing. A Resettlement Policy Framework was prepared alongside the Stage 1 plan, to be applied to Stage 2 resettlement, and a separate Resettlement Audit was commissioned to examine resettlement already done and to inform retroactive measures needed to bring it up to the Bank's involuntary resettlement policy. A three-step grievance procedure was set out in the plan; the practice at the time was a single-instance mechanism run by the Resettlement Unit, with a journal of complaints, named officials at each new site and a telephone line (Resettlement Action Plan for Stage 1, 28 August 2014; Implementation Completion and Results Report, 29 June 2015; ICR Review ICRR14942, 9 June 2016).

lenders.name: World Bank (IDA)
lenders.role: Credit 3889-GH, written IDA-38890 in the completion report, of SDR 41.6 million for the Second Urban Environmental Sanitation Project (P082373). Approved 29 April 2004 and signed 13 August 2004. The dollar equivalent is given as US$62.0 million by the completion report and the Project Performance Assessment Report and as US$64.39 million by the Inspection Panel's investigation report. US$25.7 million was allocated to the solid waste management component, of which the Kwabenya sanitary landfill was a subcomponent with base costs estimated at US$9.5 million. Closing was extended from 30 June 2010 to 31 December 2012. The credit was restructured three times; the third restructuring, approved 18 December 2012, extended closing by seven months and added a new disbursement category, Compensation Payments to Project Affected Persons, so that credit proceeds could pay compensation under the Kwabenya plan. The project cost table records US$0.18 million actually spent on compensation against nothing at appraisal. The completion report of 27 June 2013 rated outcome Moderately Satisfactory, Bank performance Moderately Satisfactory, borrower performance Moderately Satisfactory and risk to development outcome Substantial; the Independent Evaluation Group's review ICRR14631, posted 20 April 2015, gave the same first three ratings and gave risk to development outcome as Significant. The Project Performance Assessment Report of 19 May 2016 reached the same four ratings as the review and does not rate safeguards. The implementing agencies were the metropolitan and municipal assemblies of the participating cities, coordinated by a Project Coordination Unit in the Ministry of Local Government and Rural Development.

companies.name: Accra Metropolitan Assembly
companies.role: The local government authority for Accra, responsible under the Project Coordination Unit of the Ministry of Local Government and Rural Development for the city's component of the project, including the Kwabenya landfill. It requested compensation claims to be lodged with the Executive Secretary of the Land Valuation Board, told the Bank in October 2010 through the Mayor of Accra to drop Kwabenya, and listed three years of non-payment of compensation among its reasons for discontinuing the landfill.

companies.name: Ministry of Local Government and Rural Development
companies.role: The ministry responsible for local government in Ghana. Its Project Coordination Unit coordinated the components implemented by the five participating metropolitan and municipal assemblies.

kwabenya-landfill-expropriation.community: The project was to build a sanitary landfill near the village of Kwabenya to serve greater Accra, which had an estimated load of 500,000 tonnes of refuse a year. The site had been chosen for an earlier British-funded landfill from 1999; that effort built an access road and a drainage culvert and was then dropped over land right claims, and the Panel and the Project Performance Assessment Report both record that after the access road was built people moved into the area and started economic activities near the site. The Government issued an Executive Instrument on 26 January 2007 compulsorily acquiring the land, which vests it in the President free of all encumbrances, with a six-month deadline to submit compensation claims. The Panel was informed that demolition markers were painted on structures in the community in the same month, and its report includes a picture captioned 'Houses marked for demolition by National Security Authority'. In July 2007 the authorities issued a notice that rights to compensation would be forfeited if claims were not submitted by the six-month deadline. The Panel's investigation report of 13 March 2009 found that the Bank did not comply with its policies on environmental assessment, involuntary resettlement and project supervision, on the analysis of alternative sites, the analysis of impacts in the project's area of influence, environmental management planning and resettlement planning. It found that land acquisition and compensation activities started before a resettlement action plan was prepared, contrary to the project's own Resettlement Policy Framework, and that management failed to ensure that affected people were given an information sheet in a language they could read setting out the purpose of the survey or explaining the resettlement and compensation procedures. It recorded that many of the people involved were poor women working as stone quarriers who were likely to lose their livelihoods to the land acquisition, migrants with uncertain legal entitlement to be in the country, and people treated as squatters and informal quarriers with no title or permit and no legal right to compensation under local law. No Bank social scientist visited the site between 2003 and the end of 2007, the period in which relations deteriorated, and no resettlement or social safeguard specialist joined a supervision mission until the mid-term review in December 2007. At the mid-term review in October 2010 the Government asked to drop the Kwabenya site and move the funds to other activities. In April 2012 the Government asked the Bank to use credit proceeds to pay compensation for the 76 inhabited structures identified in the draft plan, undertaking to pay for the land itself, and the closing date was extended seven months to 31 December 2012 to process the payments. The payments were not completed by that date; the completion report gives as reasons that some affected people refused compensation, apparently hoping to hold on to the land, and that some said the compensation offered did not reflect inflation and current market values. In June 2015 the Government told the Bank it would revoke the Executive Instrument on which the expropriation was based, which would restore the affected people's rights. The Panel's third and final progress report of 15 October 2015 concluded that action to complete the expropriation had stalled, that no compensation under the plan was accepted by the affected people and that some continued to build on the land, and that these actions reflected their intent to contest the expropriation and remain in place. A statement by the Agyemankata community annexed to the Bank's progress report of 29 August 2011 says that no notice was served before the Executive Instrument was published, that the Resettlement Policy Framework required compensation and resettlement before the confirming instrument was passed and this was not followed, and that 'our brothers and sisters of Agyemankata were given ten (10) days to leave their own homes without compensation. National Security gave the order.' The same statement says the Okaidja Gbeke family lodged compensation claims with the Land Valuation Board as the Accra Metropolitan Assembly required, on pain of forfeiting compensation, and had received no money and heard nothing, and it cites a Ghanaian Times report of 12 October 2009 headlined '35 Houses on G.A.E.C. Land demolished' in disputing an official statement that the land for the landfill site had been paid for.
kwabenya-landfill-expropriation.displaced_note: ICIJ gives 516 for this project, which is its count of project-affected people and not a count of people moved. No Bank document found gives a count of people relocated, and the landfill was never built. The nearest figure in the Bank's documents is the 76 inhabited structures identified in the draft Resettlement Action Plan, which is a count of structures and not of people.
kwabenya-landfill-expropriation.suppression: Members of the community told the Panel during its eligibility visit that authorities came in January 2007 accompanied by 'armed policemen and national security' and marked their houses to be vacated, and that they had lost trust in the process. The Panel's own findings record that in September 2007 the Bank office and the Government agreed that work on the resettlement plan could proceed, despite the worsening safety situation, following the publication of the Executive Instrument in February 2007 and 'the marking of houses for possession in an operation supported by armed police'. The July 2007 notice that compensation rights would be forfeited if claims were not lodged by the deadline was seen by the requesters as a threat to their rights. The Panel also recorded Bank management's response, which quoted the Government's account that when officials delivered letters to members of the community in June 2004 inviting them to a meeting they 'were detained for several hours, confronted with death threats should they ever return, and the letters were returned unopened', and that since that incident government delegations, project staff, surveyors and valuation staff had visited the site under the protection of armed security personnel. The Panel found that the Bank and the Government tried to consult a broad spectrum of potentially affected people but failed to reach the Agyemankata group, which would not attend public hearings.
kwabenya-landfill-expropriation.outcome: The landfill was dropped at the mid-term review in October 2010 and the money moved to other activities, including landfills at Tema and Sekondi-Takoradi. The credit closed on 31 December 2012 with the compensation unpaid. In June 2015 the Government said it would revoke the Executive Instrument, restoring the affected people's rights, and the Bank treated that as resolving the requesters' concerns and the outstanding item in the management action plan. The Panel issued its third and final progress report on 15 October 2015. The Bank told the Independent Evaluation Group that it would keep following up with the Government on enacting the cancellation and would issue a final note.

kwabenya-landfill-expropriation.conditions: The project was a repeater of the first Urban Environmental Sanitation Project and used that project's streamlined procedures, although the first project did not include the Kwabenya landfill. The environmental and social assessment for the landfill used the 1999 British-financed environmental assessment as its basis; management acknowledged that at the time of that assessment there were 'virtually no resettlement needs' and that people moved closer to the site after the access road was built. A Resettlement Policy Framework was reviewed at appraisal and found by management to be in line with the Bank's involuntary resettlement policy, while the Bank's own Quality at Entry Assessment called it 'somewhat disorganized, unfocused, vague and repetitive, and insufficiently operational' and said the team appeared to have underestimated the grounds of remaining objections at Kwabenya. The Development Credit Agreement required a detailed resettlement action plan acceptable to the Bank, and the obligation to compensate affected people in accordance with Bank policy survived the abandonment of the landfill and the closing of the project, as did the Bank's supervision obligations. The framework itself provided that compensation and resettlement should be carried out before the confirming instrument on the land acquisition was passed; the Panel found that sequencing was not followed. The Bank insisted that compensation be paid only after the resettlement action plan was completed and accepted and, according to the Accra Metropolitan Assembly's own note, later said the environmental impact assessment should be completed before payment (Project Appraisal Document, 5 April 2004; Inspection Panel Investigation Report, 13 March 2009; Progress Report to the Board, 29 August 2011; Implementation Completion and Results Report, 27 June 2013).

The Inspection Panel's investigation report gives the total project cost as about US$173.1 million and the Independent Evaluation Group's review gives US$173.10 million at appraisal and US$176.50 million actual; the completion report's cost annex gives total project costs of US$126.70 million at appraisal and US$126.4 million actual, the figure its financing table records as the Bank loan, with resettlement entered as zero in both columns. The loan paid to upgrade 130 km of Road 19 in Santa Fe into a four-lane highway; the remaining 6 km in Cordoba were funded by the National Road Directorate. The province was to expropriate land to reach a right of way of 120 metres. The completion report of 24 June 2013 rated outcome Satisfactory, risk to development outcome Moderate, Bank performance Satisfactory and borrower performance Satisfactory. The Independent Evaluation Group's review ICRR14284, posted 24 March 2014, agreed on outcome, risk to development outcome and borrower performance and gave overall Bank performance as Moderately Satisfactory, noting that the environmental and social management plan was not fully in compliance.

companies.name: Direccion Provincial de Vialidad, Province of Santa Fe
companies.role: The provincial roads directorate of Santa Fe, which carried out the expropriations and the land and structure valuations. Its staff visited landowners, and the Project Implementation Unit inside it ran the Resettlement and Expropriation Plan and reported monthly to the Bank's task team leader.

companies.name: Direccion Nacional de Vialidad
companies.role: Argentina's national roads directorate, which funded the 6 km of Road 19 inside Cordoba province and had carried out 69 expropriations along the same road in 1972; encroachments on that earlier right of way were notified to it and to the contractor in the second half of 2008.

santa-fe-road-19-expropriation.community: The project widened 136 km of Road 19 between Santo Tome in Santa Fe and San Francisco in Cordoba, 130 km of it with Bank money, by building a second carriageway and taking land to reach a 120-metre right of way. The completion report states that 246 parcels were expropriated. The province's own completion report, summarised in the annexes of the Bank's, breaks those down into 208, or 84 per cent, taken by agreement, 33, or 14 per cent, through the courts, 2, or 0.8 per cent, state land, and 3, or 1.2 per cent, in the end not affected. Twenty additional expropriations were identified during the works and were almost finished at project closure. The report also records that 17 cases of families in vulnerable socio-economic conditions were dealt with, and that the programme to maintain the socio-economic conditions of the 26 families and economic units on expropriated parcels was completed towards the end of 2009, with the Project Management Unit monitoring cases into early 2010. School No. 1303, General Jose de San Martin, at San Agustin, stood inside the right of way; it was rebuilt with provincial funds and was operating in March 2010. The access road to Agro-Technical School No. 299 was paved for 2.5 km, finished in mid-2011, to offset the taking of part of that school's land. Two residents of Franck submitted a Request for Inspection on 7 September 2007 on their own behalf and on behalf of ten other residents who signed it, over the road's drainage design and flood risk, the amount of land taken and the compensation for it, and the consultation process; they also raised discrimination and intimidation in the land acquisition process. The Panel's investigation report of 2 July 2008 found that the Resettlement Action Plan complied with the involuntary resettlement policy for the 26 cases where more than 40 per cent of the land was taken or where there were improvements on it, because those were analysed in depth and given a socio-economic restoration programme. For properties where less than 40 per cent was taken and there were no improvements, the plan gathered only cadastral and land use data; the Panel was not shown evidence that a policy-consistent socio-economic analysis of the impact of losing a fraction of land was prepared, nor that consultations with those landowners during preparation sufficiently addressed the negative effects of partial expropriation, and it found that the lack of a complete socio-economic analysis covering all people affected by land acquisition was not consistent with the policy. The Panel went on to find that although there was only partial compliance with that policy at the start, communication with landowners improved significantly during implementation, some measures to address the effects of the partial taking were provided for, and the project was by then in compliance with it. Bank staff told the Panel that partial expropriation was compensated even though no detailed socio-economic study was carried out, that landowners were offered expropriation of the whole property where the remainder would no longer be economically viable, and that owners outside the restoration programme were offered technical advice, information on provincial productive projects and help coordinating with local business; the Panel learned that some of this was offered only recently, after social and communication experts were added to the Project Implementation Unit. The Panel heard complaints from requesters and others that pressure had been applied to accept compensation offers they considered below market value, and in other cases that owners had not been visited and had only received written notice. Other affected people said they were discriminated against because the value offered for their land was lower than for neighbouring land; management acknowledged that the soil classification maps which could have explained different values on adjoining holdings were not shared with landowners, which the Panel found generated perceptions of unfairness. One person told the Panel that a number of elderly people, including his own father, had accepted what he considered low offers because they feared being taken to court if they refused. Opinions among affected people differed: one said a counter-offer won him improved compensation, and another said that talking to others along the right of way helped them collectively judge market value and get reasonable compensation. At the time of the Panel's visit the Project Implementation Unit said 195 cash compensation agreements had been signed, 34 were under judicial review, two properties were state-owned schools, one was no longer affected because the road was changed, and 13 cases were still being processed. On the flooding claims, the Panel found the assessment of effects upstream of the road appropriate but found the Bank in non-compliance on downstream flooding, and considered that the methodologies the engineering firms used were not homogeneous and that the evidence did not support a conclusion that the upgrade would not harm affected people. A further study was commissioned in November 2009 under the management action plan. The completion report states that studies verified the adequacy of the designs but did so at the limit of capacity, so that drainage could collapse if rainfall exceeded the levels seen in March 2007, and that additional drainage works were added at Los Cuatro Sauces, Canada del Sauce and Arroyo del Sauce. Residents submitted a fourth Request for Inspection in September 2011, which the Panel did not register because implementation was almost complete with disbursements above 95 per cent; the Project Management Unit agreed to add measures to address the residents' perception of risk.
santa-fe-road-19-expropriation.displaced_note: ICIJ gives 305 for this project, which is its count of project-affected people and not a count of people moved. No Bank document found gives a count of people relocated. The counts in the Bank's own documents are of parcels and cases: 246 parcels expropriated, 26 families and economic units in the socio-economic restoration programme, 17 cases of families in vulnerable conditions dealt with, and one school rebuilt.
santa-fe-road-19-expropriation.suppression: The requesters alleged discrimination and intimidating notices during the expropriation process. The Panel did not find any evidence of intimidating notices having been sent to landowners, and said the only written communication it saw was a sample letter of 26 December 2006 sent by the Project Implementation Unit to everyone whose land was to be expropriated, telling them they would be visited and pointing them to the plan on the website. The Panel did find it possible that some landowners were not given sufficient opportunity to consider their options and may have felt pressured into accepting offers. Bank management said it took any allegation of discrimination and intimidation very seriously and would follow up closely. The Project Implementation Unit told the Panel that checks existed inside the provincial roads directorate, including an audit by the Tribunal de Cuentas each time a payment was approved, that all affected people had been told about an appeal route through the provincial ombudsman, and that the ombudsman had received no complaints. Bank staff in Washington sampled five case files at the directorate and found no evidence that expropriation and valuation procedures had not been followed.
santa-fe-road-19-expropriation.outcome: The loan closed on 30 June 2012 on its original date. The completion report rated the outcome Satisfactory and records recurrent conflict over land valuations, with owners putting very high values on their land as commodity prices rose, and says the province tried where it could to compensate owners further through complementary works such as improved accesses and small infrastructure. The Panel's investigation found the Bank in non-compliance on downstream flood assessment and on information given during land acquisition, and found that information sharing and consultation improved over time; it recorded that some requesters told it the expropriation process eventually concluded to their satisfaction. A management action plan was carried out and a progress report went to the Board on 14 June 2010.

santa-fe-road-19-expropriation.conditions: The project was prepared with a detailed environmental and social management plan and a Resettlement and Expropriation Plan. The province was to expropriate land to reach a right of way of 120 metres, under provincial legislation that allowed a landowner to have the whole property expropriated where a partial taking left the remainder economically unviable. The resettlement plan divided impacts into total or partial loss of land, loss of housing, and total or partial loss of income, and ran a socio-economic analysis only on properties where more than 40 per cent of the land was taken or where there were improvements such as housing on the land; within those, a survey identified the families needing resettlement assistance and a programme called Re-establishment of Socio-Economic Conditions of the Affected Population was prepared for the 26 cases. Bank staff worked with the Project Implementation Unit to build a matrix tracking the expropriation of every property, which the unit updated and Bank staff reviewed on periodic visits, and the unit sent the task team leader a monthly report on implementation of the plan. Affected people were told of an appeal route through the provincial ombudsman's office, and each compensation payment was audited by the Tribunal de Cuentas when approved (Inspection Panel Investigation Report, 2 July 2008; Implementation Completion and Results Report, 24 June 2013).

sutp-brts-corridor-displacement.community: The project built bus corridors and bus rapid transit systems in several Indian cities. The completion report states that land acquisition took 75 hectares of private land, affecting more than 11,000 landowners, and physically displaced 425 families, and that about 500 tenants and informal settlers were also affected. At appraisal, impacts had been envisaged for only about 1,200 people in Pimpri-Chinchwad. In Pimpri-Chinchwad the project took private land from more than 10,000 landowners and displaced 400 families, 144 of them informal settlers. The report lists the difficulties there as inordinate delays in resettlement, delays in payment of compensation, prolonged court cases, a longer stay of displaced families in a transit camp, and delays in handing land to contractors. Compliance with the involuntary resettlement policy at that subproject was rated Unsatisfactory or Moderately Unsatisfactory for three years, from July 2015 to March 2018, because of non-compliance with payment of compensation and delays in shifting displaced families. Compensation for about 80 per cent of the 10,000 affected landowners was deposited in the courts for want of ownership documents. In Hubli-Dharwad the project acquired 30 acres affecting 1,043 landowners and 500 tenants and informal settlers and displaced 21 families; the report names compensation rates for private land, resistance from religious trustees to relocating affected places of worship, and compensation for road margin areas as the key difficulties, and calls the relocation of affected workshop premises one of the hardest parts. In Naya Raipur four displaced families were given alternative housing under a government scheme and three affected small shopkeepers were given shops on a rental basis. The report also records that the project brought more than 700 untitled holders into resettlement assistance who would otherwise have been left out, and that 110 households were given security of tenure to their resettled homes in Pimpri-Chinchwad. At the time the completion report was written, compensation was still owed to 7 landowners and resettlement to 9 informal families in Pimpri-Chinchwad, and compensation to 33 landowners and resettlement assistance to 7 tenants in Hubli-Dharwad; the report attributes those delays to the people concerned not being available to receive compensation or to a lack of ownership documents, and concludes that compliance with the involuntary resettlement policy 'was met with prolonged delays'. The Independent Evaluation Group records a later position given to it by the project team in May 2019: in Pimpri-Chinchwad compensation was pending for 5 landowners out of 230 for want of ownership documents and allotment of alternative houses was pending for 5 families out of 401; in Hubli compensation had been paid to all landowners except 131 out of 1,043, who had refused the offer and gone to court for a review, with their compensation deposited in court; and resettlement assistance for 8 tenants out of about 500 was no longer needed because the corridor was finished inside the existing right of way. Those figures were attributed to the project team, not to a document, and the landowner totals they use for Pimpri-Chinchwad differ from the more than 10,000 in the completion report.

sutp-brts-corridor-displacement.displaced_note: ICIJ gives 5,564 for this project, which is its count of project-affected people and not a count of people moved. The Bank's completion report counts 425 families physically displaced: 400 in Pimpri-Chinchwad including 144 informal settlers, 21 in Hubli-Dharwad and 4 in Naya Raipur. The same report counts more than 11,000 landowners affected by the taking of 75 hectares of private land, and about 500 tenants and informal settlers affected, which are counts of people affected and not of people moved. The project team later told the Independent Evaluation Group that the Pimpri-Chinchwad figure was 401 families.
sutp-brts-corridor-displacement.outcome: The loan closed on 31 March 2018, three years and four months after its original closing date, with compensation and resettlement still outstanding for 7 landowners and 9 informal families in Pimpri-Chinchwad and 33 landowners and 7 tenants in Hubli-Dharwad. The completion report of 25 March 2019 rated the outcome Moderately Satisfactory and the Independent Evaluation Group's review agreed. The review carries a position given by the project team in May 2019 under which most of those balances had narrowed, with 131 Hubli landowners out of 1,043 refusing the compensation offered and seeking a court review.

The report names no displaced family, does not say how long the families stayed in the transit camp or where it was, and does not say how many people the 425 families contained. The review states that the project suffered from a rushed Resettlement Action Plan and Environmental Management Plan. Involuntary resettlement compliance was rated Unsatisfactory or Moderately Unsatisfactory from July 2015 to March 2018 for the Pimpri-Chinchwad subproject (Implementation Completion and Results Report, 25 March 2019; ICR Review ICRR0021663, 21 June 2019).

lenders.name: World Bank (IDA)
lenders.role: Credit IDA-44550 of SDR 115.4 million (US$190 million equivalent) and Credit IDA-51850 of SDR 64.9 million (US$100 million equivalent) for the Second Central Transport Corridor Project (P103633), the second credit being the additional financing approved 15 January 2013 and carried under its own number P124114. Approved 27 May 2008, effective 28 November 2008, mid-term review 30 July 2010, closing extended from 31 December 2011 to 31 December 2016. The project financed Phase 1 of the Dar es Salaam bus rapid transit system and work at Tanzanian airports. The Government of Tanzania was to finance resettlement, entered in the completion report's cost and financing tables at US$10.7 million both at appraisal and at the additional financing, of which US$10.3 million, 96.2 per cent, was spent; a footnote elsewhere in the same report gives the Government's resettlement contribution as US$10.0 million. Environmental Assessment (OP/BP 4.01) and Involuntary Resettlement (OP/BP 4.12) were triggered. The completion report of 7 November 2017 rated outcome Moderately Satisfactory, risk to development outcome Substantial, Bank performance Moderately Satisfactory, with quality at entry Moderately Unsatisfactory and quality of supervision Moderately Satisfactory, and borrower performance Moderately Unsatisfactory. The Independent Evaluation Group's review ICRR0021021 recorded the same ratings with no disagreement and rated the quality of the completion report Substantial. The implementing agencies were the Dar Rapid Transit Agency and the Tanzania National Roads Agency.

companies.name: Tanzania National Roads Agency
companies.role: The executive agency responsible for Tanzania's trunk and regional roads, which held fiduciary oversight of the project and ran the works contracts. The completion report says the census of project-affected people and property valuation were done before contractors were engaged, and that the agency's own account credits the Bank's local office with a leadership role among donors.

companies.name: Dar Rapid Transit Agency
companies.role: The government agency set up to deliver and oversee the bus rapid transit system in Dar es Salaam, named in the completion report as an implementing agency alongside the roads agency.

dar-brt-kariakoo-clearance.community: The project built the first phase of the Dar es Salaam bus rapid transit system, which required a terminal at Kariakoo and a bus depot at Ubungo. The completion report states that the total number of project-affected people was 877 at the start and later rose to 1,236, and that the actual resettlement plan budget was TZS 23.5 billion, about US$11 million. Serious problems emerged with compensation. In January 2011, on an implementation support mission, the Bank team learned that insufficient funds had been allocated to meet the commitments under the resettlement plan. The inadequate funding and legal disputes, including a court injunction, led to contractual disputes and the termination of two works contracts, for the Kariakoo terminal and the Ubungo depot, because the sites were not available to the contractors. Two feeder transfer stations were not acquired at all and the operational design had to be changed. The plan was updated in March 2012 and the Ministry of Finance increased the money available, and the Government introduced a communications outreach strategy and set up a grievance redress mechanism. The people affected at the Kariakoo terminal site had filed a court case in 2008 and obtained an injunction blocking the Government from accessing the site. The completion report states that the site, with 106 families in semidetached buildings, was nonetheless cleared by the Government in March 2012 after the High Court dismissed their application for an injunction on technical grounds. They filed a separate civil suit and sought a further injunction, and in December 2013 the High Court ruled formally releasing the site to the Government for public use as the terminal, while the main suit was still pending judgment. The report records that the main case was still pending judgment in 2017, eight years after it was filed. It also states that the compensation funds were deposited in an escrow account and that most of the affected people had already claimed their compensation, and that a Tanzanian practising lawyer attended the court hearings as an observer for the Bank. The report says insufficient funding was set aside for the costs of compensation and relocation of project-affected people. Phase 1 of the system was expected to displace 1,800 existing minibuses, known as daladala, whose owners were to be compensated through preferential access to bus rapid transit routes and through payment for scrapped vehicles; the report says only a fraction of the daladala had been displaced as of end-2016. After initial construction, flash flooding occurred at Jangwani along the Msimbazi river basin, which analysis attributed to rapid siltation of the basin from uncontrolled encroachment, solid waste and human activity upstream; flood prevention measures were taken, and a more permanent solution involving the relocation of petty traders was left to later phases.
dar-brt-kariakoo-clearance.displaced_label: families cleared from the Kariakoo terminal site in March 2012, World Bank completion report of 7 November 2017
dar-brt-kariakoo-clearance.displaced_note: ICIJ gives 2,862 for this project, which is its count of project-affected people and not a count of people moved. The Bank's completion report counts 106 families in semidetached buildings at the Kariakoo terminal site, cleared by the Government in March 2012. The same report gives 877 project-affected people at the start, rising to 1,236, which is a count of people affected and not of people moved.
dar-brt-kariakoo-clearance.outcome: The credits closed on 31 December 2016, five years after the original date. The completion report of 7 November 2017 rated the outcome Moderately Satisfactory and borrower performance Moderately Unsatisfactory, and the Independent Evaluation Group's review agreed on both. The main court case brought by the people cleared from the Kariakoo site in 2008 was still awaiting judgment when the report was written in 2017; their compensation had been placed in escrow and the report says most of the affected people had claimed it. The report says that for later phases of the system the compensation resources are to be in place before works begin, and draws the lesson that adequate preparation of resettlement is a critical requirement.

The safeguard instruments were an environmental and social impact assessment and a Resettlement Action Plan built from a census, a property survey and a socio-economic survey of residents and businesses, with environmental and social management plans for all components. The Government of Tanzania was to finance resettlement costs from its own funds, entered in the completion report's cost table as US$10.7 million and in a footnote to another table as US$10.0 million. companies.role: The Kenyan commission that values and pays for land taken by compulsory acquisition. At project closure Lots 3A and 3B of the James Gichuru to Rironi section were still under valuation by the commission.

nutrip-road-compensation-arrears.community: The project widened the A104 from the James Gichuru junction in Nairobi to Rironi in Kiambu County and built bypasses at Kisumu and Meru. The second update of the resettlement plan for the James Gichuru junction to Rironi section identified 5,181 project-affected persons, 3,364 structures and 839 parcels of land, against 1,322 affected persons, 133 structures and no land acquisition identified at appraisal for the whole A104 corridor programme. The estimated cost of carrying out that plan rose from US$1.3 million to US$120 million by project completion. The completion report sets out the position on payments as at 25 April 2019. On the James Gichuru to Rironi section, sub-lot 3C had 808 affected persons of whom 133 had been paid, with KES 1,037,554,915.74 due, KES 724,124,449.47 paid and KES 313,430,466.27 outstanding; Lots 3A and 3B were still under valuation by the National Land Commission at closure. On the Kisumu Northern bypass, 507 affected persons of whom 299 had been paid, with KES 947,034,632 due, KES 277,242,405 paid and KES 669,792,227 outstanding. On the Meru bypass, 921 affected persons of whom 890 had been paid, with KES 775,149,522.94 due, KES 755,815,684.94 paid and KES 19,333,838.00 outstanding; the report says compensation there was complete apart from people with succession issues. Affected people on the James Gichuru to Rironi section petitioned the Bank on 13 December 2018 alleging delay in payment for land acquisition and the associated compensation, and raising health and safety, dust emissions, access to homes and businesses, and restoration of community water connections; a Bank team met their representatives on 19 December 2018 at their request. A fatal incident occurred on 5 October 2017 on the James Gichuru to Rironi section, which the completion report attributes to inadequate traffic management at the construction site; gaps were identified from the investigation and an action plan was prepared and carried out, but compensation to the family of the person killed had not been paid by project closure because the case was pending before the magistrate's court at Limuru. There were allegations of eviction of affected people during the works, which the roads authority denied by letter of 8 April 2019, stating that 'there has been No Eviction of Project Affected Person without compensation whatsoever.' A petition to preserve Sigona House, which the applicants said had historical and architectural value, was lodged in the High Court of Kenya; the National Museums of Kenya decided the building did not qualify as a structure of historical importance under national guidelines, and the roads authority redesigned the service road to avoid it. The Star reported on 31 May 2019 that residents and business owners along the route, organised as People Affected by the Project under its chairman Kimani Njuki, wanted the expansion halted until those affected were compensated; that houses had been marked for demolition and tenants had moved out; that supermarkets, petrol stations, hotels and shops had closed, among them a Rironi petrol station closed by Peter Mwaura of Pekangu Enterprises; and that Issac Kahura was struggling to repay a loan on two flats after his tenants left. The group had complained to the Senate and to the national human rights commission, and the Transport Cabinet Secretary had missed three Senate committee invitations, on 9, 21 and 30 May 2019. The same paper reported on 20 August 2019 that Infrastructure Principal Secretary Julius Korir said KES 12 billion was needed to pay for land and structures, that the 25 km stretch was 40 per cent complete and had stalled over the money to pay property owners, that work had continued from Gitaru to Rironi after landowners were paid KES 1.2 billion, and that the section between Gitaru and ABC was undone because of non-compensation.
nutrip-road-compensation-arrears.displaced_note: ICIJ gives 2,763 for this project, which is its count of project-affected people and not a count of people moved. No Bank document found gives a count of people relocated. The Bank's own counts are of project-affected persons, structures and parcels: 5,181 affected persons, 3,364 structures and 839 parcels on the James Gichuru to Rironi section in the second plan update, against 1,322 affected persons and 133 structures at appraisal.
nutrip-road-compensation-arrears.suppression: There were allegations of eviction of project-affected persons during the works on the James Gichuru junction to Rironi section. The Kenya National Highways Authority denied them by letter of 8 April 2019, stating that no project-affected person had been evicted without compensation. The Star reported on 31 May 2019 that houses along the route had been marked for demolition and that tenants had moved out, and did not report that any demolition had taken place.
nutrip-road-compensation-arrears.killed_note: The completion report records one fatal incident, on 5 October 2017 on the James Gichuru to Rironi section, and attributes it to inadequate traffic management at the construction site. It does not name the person, does not say whether they were a worker or a road user, and records that compensation to the family had not been paid by project closure because the case was pending before the magistrate's court at Limuru.
nutrip-road-compensation-arrears.outcome: The Government asked for the undisbursed credit to be cancelled on 21 December 2018 and the credit closed on 31 December 2018 with 22.7 per cent disbursed and many activities still running. On the Bank's own figures, 675 of the 808 affected people on sub-lot 3C of the James Gichuru to Rironi section and 208 of the 507 on the Kisumu Northern bypass were unpaid as at 25 April 2019, and two lots of the Nairobi section had not been valued. The Bank wrote to the Government on 5 March 2019 that its safeguards obligations, including carrying out all resettlement plans and setting aside adequate funds to do so, continued to bind it after the credit closed, and that the Bank would keep providing periodic oversight. The completion report rated the outcome Unsatisfactory and the Independent Evaluation Group agreed. In August 2019 the Infrastructure Principal Secretary said KES 12 billion was still needed to pay for land and structures and that part of the road was undone because people had not been compensated.

nutrip-road-compensation-arrears.confidence_note: The payment tables, the reclassification to environmental category A, the Unsatisfactory social safeguards rating, the fatal incident and the cancellation of the credit all come from the Bank's own completion report, and the Independent Evaluation Group's review of that report repeats the same facts. Two named reports in The Star corroborate independently that compensation was unpaid, that houses had been marked for demolition, that tenants had left and that businesses along the route had closed, and the second quotes a government principal secretary on the money still owed. The two newspaper reports describe the position after the credit was cancelled; the August 2019 report does not name the World Bank, and its figures do not match the Bank's tables, which cover different lots. The Bank's documents name no affected person, give no count of people relocated, and do not say what happened to the people on the lots that had not been valued at closure. The roads authority denies that anyone was evicted without compensation. The person killed on 5 October 2017 is not named and the documents do not say whether they were a worker or a road user.
nutrip-road-compensation-arrears.conditions: The project triggered Environmental Assessment (OP/BP 4.01), Involuntary Resettlement (OP/BP 4.12) and Physical Cultural Resources (OP/BP 4.11), and was appraised as environmental category B on the basis that the works were mostly rehabilitation and expansion inside existing rights of way. It was reclassified to category A once bus rapid transit was incorporated into the James Gichuru junction to Rironi section, because that required wider resettlement areas and land acquisition; the updated safeguards data sheet was approved and disclosed on 9 November 2018, but the restructuring that would have given effect to the change was never finalised and the credit was cancelled six weeks later. Resettlement action plans were prepared and updated for each section, and the second update for the Nairobi section multiplied the identified impacts and costs. The Bank's letter of 5 March 2019 confirmed that the Government's obligation to carry out the disclosed resettlement and environmental instruments, and to set aside adequate funds for them, survived the cancellation of the credit (Implementation Completion and Results Report, 26 June 2019).

lenders.name: World Bank (IDA)
lenders.role: Credits IDA-47240 and IDA-49910 for the Transport Sector Support Project (P055120), SDR 214.3 million in all, US$329 million equivalent: US$270 million under IDA-47240, of which US$266.20 million was disbursed, and US$59 million under IDA-49910, of which US$54.40 million was disbursed, the second being the additional financing approved 30 June 2011 and carried under its own number P126206. Approved 27 May 2010, effective 1 December 2010, mid-term review 5 May 2014, closing extended from 30 June 2015 to 20 June 2017. The borrower was to contribute US$11.7 million and contributed US$4.51 million, for a total project cost of US$325.12 million against US$340.7 million planned. The project financed roads under Component A and airports, including Bukoba, Kigoma, Tabora and Zanzibar, under Component B. Involuntary Resettlement (OP/BP 4.12) and Physical Cultural Resources (OP 4.11) were triggered. The completion report rated outcome Moderately Satisfactory, Bank performance Moderately Satisfactory and quality of monitoring and evaluation Modest; the Independent Evaluation Group's review ICRR0021116, dated 25 May 2018, gave the same three ratings with no disagreement recorded and rated the quality of the completion report Substantial. The implementing agencies were the Tanzania National Roads Agency and the Tanzania Airports Authority.

companies.name: Tanzania Airports Authority
companies.role: The government authority that owns and runs Tanzania's airports and was responsible for the airport component. Resettlement plans were prepared for all the airports in the project, and at project closure the entitlement agreed in the one Bukoba case settled through the grievance mechanism was still awaiting payment from this authority, which agreed to keep sending progress reports to the Bank until the remaining cases were resolved.

companies.name: Tanzania National Roads Agency
companies.role: The executive agency responsible for Tanzania's trunk and regional roads, which implemented the road component and held fiduciary responsibility for the project, and which hired three additional procurement staff for it.

bukoba-airport-resettlement-arrears.community: The project paved and improved runways, taxiways, aprons and terminals at Bukoba, Kigoma, Tabora and Zanzibar airports and rehabilitated road lengths. The completion report rates the project's social safeguard management satisfactory. It states that resettlement plans were prepared for all the airports, that no resettlement was required at Tabora or Kigoma, that resettlement at Zanzibar airport was completed, and that at Bukoba five resettlement cases remained pending at project closure. Four of those five were awaiting court deliberations. The fifth had been resolved through the project's grievance redress mechanism, with the entitlement agreed and payment still pending from the Tanzania Airports Authority. The authority agreed to keep submitting progress reports to the Bank until the remaining cases were resolved. During implementation it was found that Tumaini Primary School, a public primary school serving the area around Bukoba airport and hosting a unit for more than 50 disabled children, stood within the flight path of the extended runway. Flight restrictions were imposed so that operations were allowed only in the direction away from the school, and it was decided that the school had to be relocated. Empty land was contributed by the local government, new school buildings were put up, and both former and new students began attending in the new location; the original school was demolished and its land demarcated. The completion report says there were some students whose commute was made more challenging but that the move was largely successful, and that the airports authority and the Bukoba airport management committed to continue supporting the school. On the road component, the lengths were built inside existing alignments and no resettlement was found to be required; the 7 km stretch of the Arusha to Minjingo road inside Arusha town was left out of the civil works at preparation because resettlement would have been needed there, although the detailed designs for it were finished. During implementation several families living near a quarry used by the Arusha to Minjingo contractor asked to be relocated; the report says their request was met and they were relocated. At Zanzibar airport the extension of the taxiway required a cemetery to be relocated, which the report says was done satisfactorily. No archaeologist was engaged as the project had expected, although the report says very little undisturbed land was used and no chance finds were identified.
bukoba-airport-resettlement-arrears.displaced_note: ICIJ gives 3,595 for this project, which is its count of project-affected people and not a count of people moved. No Bank document found gives a count of people relocated. The only figures in the Bank's documents are five resettlement cases still pending at Bukoba at project closure, four of them in court, and several unnumbered families near a quarry on the Arusha to Minjingo road who asked to be relocated and were.
bukoba-airport-resettlement-arrears.outcome: The credits closed on 20 June 2017, two years after the original closing date. Five resettlement cases at Bukoba were still unresolved at closure, four of them before the courts and one with payment outstanding. The Independent Evaluation Group's review records that the project team subsequently told it that the high court cases on carrying out the resettlement plan had been ruled on and that payment of compensation to the affected people was being processed; that statement is attributed to the project team and not to a document. The completion report of 16 January 2018 rated the outcome Moderately Satisfactory and the Independent Evaluation Group agreed.

bukoba-airport-resettlement-arrears.confidence_note: Everything here comes from the Bank's own completion report on its own project and from the Independent Evaluation Group's review of that report. No independent source on the Bukoba resettlement cases or the school was found. The documents give no count of people, name nobody, do not say how much the outstanding entitlement was or what the four court cases were about, and do not say how many students' journeys to school became longer. The later statement that the court cases had been decided and payment was being processed is attributed to the project team rather than to a document. The completion report also says the school move was largely successful, that the families near the quarry asked to move and were satisfied, and that the Zanzibar resettlement was completed. The completion report's cover page is dated January 16, 2017, five months before the closing date of 20 June 2017 that its own data sheet gives; the Independent Evaluation Group's review states that the date on the front page should be 2018 and not 2017, and the report's exchange rate is given as effective 27 December 2017.
bukoba-airport-resettlement-arrears.conditions: The project triggered Involuntary Resettlement (OP/BP 4.12) and Physical Cultural Resources (OP 4.11). Resettlement action plans were prepared for every airport in the project. The 7 km of the Arusha to Minjingo road inside Arusha town was deliberately excluded from the civil works at preparation because resettlement would have been required there, while the detailed designs for a later rehabilitation were completed. The project was expected to engage an archaeologist to assess chance finds under the cultural property policy and did not do so. Construction companies were required to put in place HIV prevention education and sensitisation plans, including voluntary testing, in collaboration with district health officers (Implementation Completion and Results Report, 16 January 2018; ICR Review ICRR0021116, 25 May 2018).
